title: Prenatal blood screening
what: Blood is taken from the mother's vein to measure special proteins and hormones. Together with an ultrasound, this helps estimate the risk of some conditions in the baby.
why: For all pregnant women at set times: usually at 11 to 14 weeks, and sometimes in the second trimester.
duration: the blood draw takes 3 to 5 minutes; results usually come in 2 to 7 days
tell_doctor: Exactly how far along you are and your latest ultrasound results
If you are carrying twins or conceived through IVF
Your exact weight. It is used in the calculation

prepare.title: Timing
prepare.text: Blood is taken at the time your doctor set, often on the same day as the screening ultrasound or close to it.

prepare.title: Food
prepare.text: Usually fasting, or a few hours after a light meal. Better to avoid fatty food the day before. Check with the clinic.

prepare.title: Clothing
prepare.text: Wear a sleeve that is easy to roll up above the elbow.

steps: You fill out a form: weeks of pregnancy, weight, and height
You sit down and rest your arm on the armrest
A band is tightened above your elbow, and the skin is wiped
Blood is drawn into a tube
The needle comes out, and a cotton pad is pressed on
feel: A quick prick, like a pinch
The test is safe for the baby
after: Press the cotton pad for 3 to 5 minutes
Results usually come in 2 to 7 days. It is a risk estimate, not a diagnosis
If the risk is high, your doctor will offer more tests

faq.q: Does a high risk mean the baby has a condition?
faq.a: No. It means more checking is needed. Most women with a high-risk result have a healthy baby.

faq.q: Why does the exact week matter?
faq.a: Protein levels change every week. If the dates are off, the risk estimate will be wrong.

reminders.text: Prenatal screening tomorrow. Bring your ultrasound report and check if you need to come fasting.
